claim: Portions of Drosophila melanogaster larval nociceptive class IV dendrite arborization (da) neuron dendrites become ensheathed by epidermal cells.
source: Notably, portions of Drosophila melanogaster larval nociceptive class IV dendrite arborization (da) neuron dendrites and Danio rerio (zebrafish) larval trigeminal and Rohon-Beard (RB) sensory axons become ensheathed by epidermal cells (Han et al., 2012; Kim et al., 2012; O'Brien et al., 2012)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior published work (Han et al., 2012; Kim et al., 2012; O'Brien et al., 2012).

claim: Danio rerio (zebrafish) larval trigeminal and Rohon-Beard (RB) sensory axons become ensheathed by epidermal cells.

evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior published work (Han et al., 2012; Kim et al., 2012; O'Brien et al., 2012).

claim: Drosophila and zebrafish epidermal cells wrap sensory neurites by extending membranes around the entire circumference of the sensory neurite.

claim: The wrapping epidermal membranes are tightly apposed to one another and the ensheathed neurites, embedding them inside a mesaxon-like structure.
source: The wrapping epidermal membranes are tightly apposed to one another and the ensheathed neurites, embedding them inside a mesaxon-like structure (Whitear and Moate, 1998; Han et al., 2012; Kim et al., 2012; O'Brien et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior published work (Whitear and Moate, 1998; Han et al., 2012; Kim et al., 2012; O'Brien et al., 2012).

claim: A similar structure has been documented for ensheathed somatosensory neurites in Caenorhabditis elegans and humans.
source: A similar structure has been documented for ensheathed somatosensory neurites in Caenorhabditis elegans and humans (Cauna, 1973; Chalfie and Sulston, 1981)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior published work (Cauna, 1973; Chalfie and Sulston, 1981).

claim: Ensheathment by epidermal cells is a conserved feature of sensory endings.
source: A similar structure has been documented for ensheathed somatosensory neurites in Caenorhabditis elegans and humans (Cauna, 1973; Chalfie and Sulston, 1981), suggesting that ensheathment by epidermal cells is a conserved feature of sensory endings.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that similar structures exist across multiple species (C. elegans, humans, Drosophila, zebrafish), as supported by citations.

claim: The sensory neurites can be continuously ensheathed over extended lengths of the arbor, stretching several micrometers or more.

evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior published work (O'Brien et al., 2012).

claim: Keratinocyte ensheathment may regulate sensory neuron structure.
source: Structurally, the interaction between keratinocytes and somatosensory neurites is reminiscent of ensheathment of peripheral axons by nonmyelinating Schwann cells in Remak bundles, suggesting that keratinocyte ensheathment may likewise regulate sensory neuron structure (Chen et al., 2003) and function (Orita et al., 2013; Faroni et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the structural similarity to Schwann cell ensheathment, which is known to regulate neuron structure, and is supported by citations (Chen et al., 2003; Orita et al., 2013; Faroni et al., 2014).

claim: Keratinocyte ensheathment may regulate sensory neuron function.

evidence: The claim is inferred from the structural similarity to Schwann cell ensheathment, which is known to regulate neuron function, and is supported by citations (Chen et al., 2003; Orita et al., 2013; Faroni et al., 2014).

claim: Dendrites were embedded in epithelial cells over extended distances (often several microns or more).
source: We found that dendrites were embedded in epithelial cells over extended distances (often several microns or more), that dendrites were continuously embedded in these mesaxon-like structures with elongated tubular invaginations, and that the epidermal membranes comprising the walls of these tubular invaginations were tightly juxtaposed and electron-dense along their entire length (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by SBF-SEM data presented in Figure 1B and C.

claim: Dendrites were continuously embedded in mesaxon-like structures with elongated tubular invaginations.

claim: The epidermal membranes comprising the walls of tubular invaginations were tightly juxtaposed and electron-dense along their entire length.

claim: PLCδ-PH-GFP accumulated at epithelial cell-cell junctions, punctate patches, and elongated filamentous membrane microdomains adjacent to c4da dendrites.

claim: PIP2 microdomains correspond to epidermal dendrite sheaths.
source: These PIP2 microdomains were also labeled by antibodies to the Drosophila 4.1 protein cora (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), a previously described marker of epidermal dendrite sheaths (Kim et al., 2012; Tenenbaum et al., 2017), demonstrating that these PIP2 microdomains correspond to epidermal dendrite sheaths.
evidence: The claim is supported by co-localization data with cora, a known sheath marker, as shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and supported by citations (Kim et al., 2012; Tenenbaum et al., 2017).

claim: PLCδ-PH-GFP labeled membrane domains that often appeared wider than c4da dendrites.
source: PLCδ-PH-GFP labeled membrane domains that often appeared wider than c4da dendrites (Figure 1H–1I), suggesting that PIP2 labels the entire sheath structure, including the convoluted tubular extensions to the basal surface of the epidermis.
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data presented in Figure 1H-1I.

claim: PIP2 labels the entire sheath structure, including the convoluted tubular extensions to the basal surface of the epidermis.

claim: The intensity of HRP labeling along dendrites was inversely related to GFP labeling intensity.

claim: PLCδ-PH-GFP labeled epidermal structures that extend from the most apical extent of dendrite insertion to the basal surface of individual epithelial cells.

claim: PLCδ-PH-GFP was locally depleted at branch points.

evidence: The claim is supported by expansion microscopy data presented in Figure 1J and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D, and is consistent with prior observations cited (Tenenbaum et al., 2017).

evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and citations describing the mutations (Várnai and Balla, 1998; Verstreken et al., 2009).

claim: Epithelial sites of dendrite ensheathment are enriched in PIP2.

claim: Drosophila and zebrafish epidermal sheaths are similar in ultrastructure and molecular composition.
source: Taken together, our results demonstrate similarity in ultrastructure and molecular composition of Drosophila and zebrafish epidermal sheaths, suggesting that these structures form via an evolutionarily conserved pathway.

claim: Nociceptive c4da neurons exhibited the most extensive ensheathment among multi-dendritic da neurons.

evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data presented in Figure 3D-3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Mechanosensitive and thermosensitive c3da and c2da neurons exhibited an intermediate level of ensheathment.

claim: Different individual sensory neurons in zebrafish were ensheathed to different degrees.

claim: The degree of ensheathment appeared to correlate with axon arbor complexity in zebrafish: axons with fewer branches associated with α-catenin along a greater proportion of their length (up to ~80% axon length) than did highly complex axons (<30% axon length).

claim: The degree of axon ensheathment may be a subtype-specific feature in zebrafish.

claim: C4da dendrites tile the larval body wall by ~36 h after egg laying (AEL).

claim: PIP2 first accumulated in isolated patches adjacent to dendrites at 48 h AEL.

evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data presented in Figure 4A-4C and 4G.

claim: Epidermal PIP2 did not co-occur with large portions of the dendrite arbor until after 96 hAEL.
source: Epidermal PIP2 did not co-occur with large portions of the dendrite arbor until after 96 hAEL (Figure 4D–4F and G), a time point at which dendrites are internalized in epithelial cells (Jiang et al., 2014; Jiang et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data presented in Figure 4D-4F and 4G, and citations (Jiang et al., 2014; Jiang et al., 2018).

claim: Once formed, PIP2-positive epidermal sheaths persist or grow, but rarely retract.
source: Furthermore, time-lapse imaging demonstrated that PIP2 enrichment at sheaths is not transient; once formed, PIP2-positive epidermal sheaths persist or grow, but rarely retract (Figure 4H, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by time-lapse confocal microscopy data presented in Figure 4H and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Cora accumulation lagged behind PLCδ-PH-GFP.
source: Finally, although PIP2 markers and cora extensively co-localized and labeled a nearly identical population of sheaths by the end of larval development (95.7 ± 5.8% of cora-positive sheaths are PIP2-positive; 88.7 ± 7.4% of PIP2-positive sheaths are cora-positive; n = 8 hemisegments), cora accumulation lagged behind PLCδ-PH-GFP (Figure 4G, Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of confocal microscopy data presented in Figure 4G and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: PIP2 accumulation marks an earlier stage in sheath formation than does cora recruitment.
source: Thus, although PIP2 accumulation marks an earlier stage in sheath formation than does cora recruitment, we found no evidence that a pre-pattern predicts the site of ensheathment.
evidence: The claim is a summary statement supported by the preceding experimental observations.

claim: There is no evidence that a pre-pattern predicts the site of ensheathment.
source: Thus, although PIP2 accumulation marks an earlier stage in sheath formation than does cora recruitment, we found no evidence that a pre-pattern predicts the site of ensheathment.
evidence: The claim is a summary statement supported by the preceding experimental observations.

claim: Expressing the pro-apoptotic gene reaper (rpr) in c4da neurons with two copies of the c4da-specific ppk-Gal4 Gal4 driver resulted in fully penetrant death and clearance of c4da neurons but not other sensory neurons by the end of the first larval instar, prior to appearance of epithelial sheaths.
source: Expressing the pro-apoptotic gene reaper (rpr) in c4da neurons with two copies of the c4da-specific ppk-Gal4 Gal4 driver (Grueber et al., 2003) resulted in fully penetrant death and clearance of c4da neurons but not other sensory neurons by the end of the first larval instar, prior to appearance of epithelial sheaths.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and a citation (Grueber et al., 2003).

claim: Anti-cora staining of larvae expressing rpr in c4da neurons revealed that although the overall extent of ensheathment was significantly reduced, levels of ensheathment in c1/c2/c3da neurons were unaffected by this treatment.
source: Anti-cora staining of these larvae revealed that although the overall extent of ensheathment was significantly reduced, levels of ensheathment in c1/c2/c3da neurons were unaffected by this treatment (cora-positive sheath length per mm2 of body wall: 2.72 ± 0.64 mm following c4da rpr expression; 11.44 ± 1.81 mm in sibling controls without rpr; 3.18 ± 1.16 mm for c1/c2/c3da neurons from sibling controls; mean ±sd, n = 8) (Figure 4I–4K).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of immunostaining data presented in Figure 4I-4K.

claim: Dendrite-derived signals induce sheath formation.
source: These results demonstrate that dendrite-derived signals induce sheath formation; such signals are likely short-range signals, as sheaths form at sites directly apposed to dendrites.
evidence: The claim is a summary statement supported by the preceding experimental observations.

claim: Dendrite-derived signals for sheath formation are likely short-range signals.
source: These results demonstrate that dendrite-derived signals induce sheath formation; such signals are likely short-range signals, as sheaths form at sites directly apposed to dendrites.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that sheaths form at sites directly apposed to dendrites.

claim: Modality-specific levels of ensheathment do not reflect competitive interactions between c4da and other da neurons for sheath formation.
source: These results further suggest that modality-specific levels of ensheathment do not reflect competitive interactions between c4da and other da neurons for sheath formation, as the absence of c4da neurons did not potentiate sheath formation in spared neurons.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that removing c4da neurons did not increase ensheathment of other da neurons.

claim: Following laser ablation of c2da, c3da, and c4da neurons at 48 h AEL, cora-positive sheaths did not form.
source: Using a focused laser beam we ablated Drosophila c2da, c3da, and c4da neurons at 48 h AEL, prior to appreciable accumulation of sheath markers or appearance of sheaths in TEM sections (Jiang et al., 2014), and assayed for sheath formation at 120 h AEL using anti-cora immunostaining. Following this treatment, cora-positive sheaths did not form (Figure 4L–4N)
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data presented in Figure 4L-4N and a citation (Jiang et al., 2014).

claim: Dendrite signals initiate sheath formation after 48 h AEL.
source: suggesting that dendrite signals initiate sheath formation after 48 h AEL, the same timeframe at which PIP2 markers first accumulate at sites of dendrite contact.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that ablation at 48 h AEL prevents sheath formation.

claim: Different neuron classes have different capacities for ensheathment.
source: These results further demonstrate that different neuron classes have different capacities for ensheathment, because removing all of the da neurons that are normally ensheathed did not potentiate c1da neuron ensheathment.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that removing ensheathed neurons did not increase ensheathment of c1da neurons.

claim: By 12 h post-severing, both the c4da dendrites distal to the cut site and the epidermal sheaths that wrapped them had disappeared.
source: By 12 h post-severing, both the c4da dendrites distal to the cut site and the epidermal sheaths that wrapped them had disappeared (Figure 4R–4T).
evidence: The claim is supported by time-lapse confocal microscopy data presented in Figure 4R-4T.

claim: Short-range dendrite-derived signals are required both for the formation and maintenance of epidermal sheaths.
source: Therefore, short-range dendrite-derived signals are required both for the formation and maintenance of epidermal sheaths.
evidence: The claim is a summary statement supported by the preceding experimental observations.

claim: Basal cells in neurog1 MO-treated zebrafish animals lacked coherent PIP2-rich microdomains, apical accumulations of F-actin, and α-catenin-containing autotypic junctions.
source: Basal cells in neurog1 MO-treated animals lacked coherent PIP2-rich microdomains, apical accumulations of F-actin, and α-catenin-containing autotypic junctions, demonstrating that epidermal sheaths are initiated by axons in zebrafish larvae (Figure 4U–4Z).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data presented in Figure 4U-4Z.

claim: Epidermal sheaths are initiated by axons in zebrafish larvae.
source: Basal cells in neurog1 MO-treated animals lacked coherent PIP2-rich microdomains, apical accumulations of F-actin, and α-catenin-containing autotypic junctions, demonstrating that epidermal sheaths are initiated by axons in zebrafish larvae (Figure 4U–4Z).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data presented in Figure 4U-4Z.

claim: Axons are required to maintain sheaths in zebrafish.
source: As in Drosophila, axons were also required to maintain sheaths, as PIP2-rich microdomains disappeared soon after laser axotomy and axon degeneration (Figure 4AA).
evidence: The claim is supported by laser axotomy data presented in Figure 4AA.

claim: From the earliest time-point that PIP2 enrichment was detectable at sheaths, dArf6-GFP enrichment was also detected, albeit at a subset of PIP2-positive sheaths.
source: From the earliest time-point that PIP2 enrichment was detectable at sheaths, we also detected dArf6-GFP enrichment, albeit at a subset of PIP2-positive sheaths, suggesting that dArf6 is recruited to sheaths shortly after PIP2 enrichment (Figure 5A–5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data presented in Figure 5A-5B.

claim: dArf6 is recruited to sheaths shortly after PIP2 enrichment.
source: From the earliest time-point that PIP2 enrichment was detectable at sheaths, we also detected dArf6-GFP enrichment, albeit at a subset of PIP2-positive sheaths, suggesting that dArf6 is recruited to sheaths shortly after PIP2 enrichment (Figure 5A–5B).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that dArf6-GFP is detected at a subset of PIP2-positive sheaths from the earliest time-point.

claim: F-actin labeling lagged behind PIP2.
source: By contrast, F-actin labeling lagged behind PIP2 (Figure 5C–5D), appearing on a comparable timescale as cora.
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data presented in Figure 5C-5D.

claim: Sheaths that were initially labeled by UAS-PLCδ-PH-Cerulean but not UAS-GFP-cora1-383 were positive for both markers following a 12 h time-lapse.
source: However, sheaths that were initially labeled by UAS-PLCδ-PH-Cerulean but not UAS-GFP-cora1-383, a GFP-tagged fusion protein that mimics endogenous cora localization at epidermal sheaths and septate junctions (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C), were positive for both markers following a 12 h time-lapse (Figure 5E–5F).
evidence: The claim is supported by time-lapse confocal microscopy data presented in Figure 5E-5F.

claim: GMA-GFP and dArf6-GFP were recruited to sheaths that were initially PIP2-positive but GFP-negative.
source: Similarly, we found that GMA-GFP and dArf6-GFP were recruited to sheaths that were initially PIP2-positive but GFP-negative (Figure 5F, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by time-lapse confocal microscopy data presented in Figure 5F and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-1B.

claim: Epidermal sheath assembly proceeds via separable steps.
source: Epidermal sheath assembly therefore appears to proceed via separable steps.
evidence: The claim is a summary statement supported by the preceding experimental observations.

claim: Membrane reporters appeared near zebrafish axons before F-actin or junctional reporters.
source: Examining ensheathment channel-associated markers at four stages of zebrafish development revealed a similar sequence of events. As in Drosophila, we found that membrane reporters appeared near zebrafish axons before F-actin or junctional reporters (Figure 5G).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data presented in Figure 5G.

claim: PIP2-rich microdomains frequently apposed axons by 32 hpf in zebrafish, before ensheathment channels were evident ultrastructurally.
source: PIP2-rich microdomains frequently apposed axons by 32 hpf, before ensheathment channels were evident ultrastructurally (O'Brien et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data and a citation (O'Brien et al., 2012).

claim: The formation of PIP2-positive membrane microdomains is an early step in sheath morphogenesis in zebrafish.
source: This observation suggests that the formation of PIP2-positive membrane microdomains is an early step in sheath morphogenesis in zebrafish, as in Drosophila.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that PIP2-rich microdomains appear before ensheathment channels are evident ultrastructurally.

claim: Time-lapse confocal microscopy demonstrated that PIP2-positive membrane microdomains formed during development just minutes after an axonal growth cone passed through that region in zebrafish.
source: Indeed, time-lapse confocal microscopy demonstrated that these domains formed during development just minutes after an axonal grown cone passed through that region (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by time-lapse confocal microscopy data presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Epidermal PI4K(RNAi) and shiDN expression severely attenuated PIP2 accumulation at sheaths.
source: We found that epidermal PI4K(RNAi) and shiDN expression severely attenuated PIP2 accumulation at sheaths (Figure 5H, Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data presented in Figure 5H and Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: Epidermal cora(RNAi) had no effect on PLCδ-PH-GFP accumulation.
source: By contrast, epidermal cora(RNAi) had no effect on PLCδ-PH-GFP accumulation, suggesting that cora accumulation is a downstream event in sheath assembly.
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data.

claim: Cora accumulation is a downstream event in sheath assembly.
source: By contrast, epidermal cora(RNAi) had no effect on PLCδ-PH-GFP accumulation, suggesting that cora accumulation is a downstream event in sheath assembly.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that cora(RNAi) does not affect PIP2 accumulation.

claim: Both epidermal PI4K(RNAi) and shiDN expression blocked cora accumulation at sheaths.
source: Consistent with this notion, both epidermal PI4K(RNAi) and shiDN expression blocked cora accumulation at sheaths (Figure 5H, Figure 5—figure supplement 3)
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data presented in Figure 5H and Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: Cora recruitment to sheaths depends on PIP2 accumulation.
source: suggesting that cora recruitment to sheaths depends on PIP2 accumulation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that blocking PIP2 accumulation blocks cora accumulation.

claim: PIP2 accumulation and cora accumulation mark genetically separable steps in sheath assembly.
source: PIP2 accumulation and cora accumulation therefore mark genetically separable steps in sheath assembly that we subsequently refer to as initiation and maturation, respectively (Figure 5I).
evidence: The claim is a summary statement supported by the preceding experimental observations and is illustrated in Figure 5I.

claim: Epidermis-specific expression of PI4K(RNAi) significantly increased the number and decreased the average length of terminal dendrites.
source: Compared to controls, epidermis-specific expression of PI4K(RNAi) significantly increased the number and decreased the average length of terminal dendrites (Figure 6A–6B and G–H).
evidence: The claim is supported by morphometric analysis of confocal microscopy data presented in Figure 6A-6B and 6G-6H.

claim: Epidermal PLCδ-PH-GFP expression increased terminal dendrite branch number and decreased dendrite branch length in a dose-dependent manner.
source: PLCδ-PH-GFP can function as a competitive inhibitor of PIP2 signaling (Raucher et al., 2000), and epidermal PLCδ-PH-GFP expression increased terminal dendrite branch number and decreased dendrite branch length in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by morphometric analysis of confocal microscopy data presented in Figure 6—figure supplement 1 and a citation (Raucher et al., 2000).

claim: Blocking epidermal endocytosis via constitutive epidermal expression of shiDN or expressing temperature sensitive shits and using it to conditionally blocking epidermal endocytosis specifically in the time window during which dendrites are normally ensheathed led to severe terminal dendrite branching defects qualitatively similar to PI4K(RNAi).
source: Similarly, blocking epidermal endocytosis via constitutive epidermal expression of shiDN or expressing temperature sensitive shits and using it to conditionally blocking epidermal endocytosis specifically in the time window during which dendrites are normally ensheathed led to severe terminal dendrite branching defects qualitatively similar to PI4K(RNAi) (Figure 6C–6D and G–H).
evidence: The claim is supported by morphometric analysis of confocal microscopy data presented in Figure 6C-6D and 6G-6H.

claim: Epidermal expression of cora(RNAi) induced growth of short terminal dendrites.
source: Finally, epidermal expression of cora(RNAi) induced growth of short terminal dendrites (Figure 6E and G–H), as has been previously reported (Tenenbaum et al., 2017)
evidence: The claim is supported by morphometric analysis of confocal microscopy data presented in Figure 6E and 6G-6H, and a citation (Tenenbaum et al., 2017).

claim: Epidermal expression of shg(RNAi) induced growth of short terminal dendrites.
source: as did epidermal expression of shg(RNAi) (Figure 6F–6H).
evidence: The claim is supported by morphometric analysis of confocal microscopy data presented in Figure 6F-6H.

claim: Blocking the early or late events of epidermal sheath formation deregulates branching morphogenesis of Drosophila nociceptive c4da neurons.
source: Thus, blocking the early or late events of epidermal sheath formation deregulates branching morphogenesis of Drosophila nociceptive c4da neurons.
evidence: The claim is a summary statement supported by the preceding experimental observations.

claim: Over an 18 h time-lapse beginning at 96 h AEL more than 80% of terminal dendrites persisted in control larvae, with the vast majority of those dendrites elongating.
source: Over an 18 h time-lapse beginning at 96 h AEL more than 80% of terminal dendrites persisted in control larvae, with the vast majority of those dendrites elongating (Figure 6I and L).
evidence: The claim is supported by time-lapse confocal microscopy data presented in Figure 6I and 6L.

claim: Using epidermis-specific expression of PI4K(RNAi) or cora(RNAi) to block sheath initiation or maturation, respectively, led to significant alterations in branch dynamics.
source: By contrast, using epidermis-specific expression of PI4K(RNAi) or cora(RNAi) to block sheath initiation or maturation, respectively, led to significant alterations in branch dynamics (Figure 6J–6L).
evidence: The claim is supported by time-lapse confocal microscopy data presented in Figure 6J-6L.

claim: A larger fraction of terminal dendrites exhibited dynamic growth behavior in PI4K(RNAi) and cora(RNAi) larvae.
source: First, a larger fraction of terminal dendrites exhibited dynamic growth behavior.
evidence: The claim is supported by time-lapse confocal microscopy data.

claim: The relative levels of growth and retraction were altered in PI4K(RNAi) and cora(RNAi) larvae; whereas growth predominated in controls, growth and retraction occurred with comparable frequency in PI4K(RNAi) and cora(RNAi) larvae.
source: Second, the relative levels of growth and retraction were altered; whereas growth predominated in controls, growth and retraction occurred with comparable frequency in PI4K(RNAi) and cora(RNAi) larvae.
evidence: The claim is supported by time-lapse confocal microscopy data.

claim: The average change in terminal dendrite length was reduced in PI4K(RNAi) and cora(RNAi) larvae.
source: Third, the average change in terminal dendrite length was reduced in PI4K(RNAi) and cora(RNAi) larvae (Figure 6M).
evidence: The claim is supported by time-lapse confocal microscopy data presented in Figure 6M.

claim: Epidermal ensheathment alters dendrite growth properties by stabilizing existing terminal dendrites and promoting their elongation.
source: These results suggest that epidermal ensheathment alters dendrite growth properties by stabilizing existing terminal dendrites and promoting their elongation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that blocking ensheathment increases dendrite dynamics and reduces elongation.

claim: Whereas >65% of terminal dendrites were present only transiently during a 12 h time lapse at the onset of ensheathment (72–84 h AEL), most terminal dendrites persisted during a 12 h time lapse after arbors were extensively ensheathed (108–120 h AEL).
source: Whereas >65% of terminal dendrites were present only transiently during a 12 h time lapse at the onset of ensheathment (72–84 h AEL), most terminal dendrites persisted during a 12 h time lapse after arbors were extensively ensheathed (108–120 h AEL) (Figure 6N).
evidence: The claim is supported by time-lapse confocal microscopy data presented in Figure 6N.

claim: A significantly higher proportion of ensheathed terminal dendrites were growing or stable over a 12 h time-lapse (108–120 h AEL).
source: In this latter time window (108–120 h AEL) we compared the growth dynamics of ensheathed and unensheathed terminal dendrites and found that a significantly higher proportion of ensheathed terminal dendrites were growing or stable over the 12 h time-lapse (Figure 6O).
evidence: The claim is supported by time-lapse confocal microscopy data presented in Figure 6O.

claim: Epidermal sheaths contribute to stabilization of somatosensory dendrites.
source: Altogether, our time-lapse imaging results strongly suggest that epidermal sheaths contribute to stabilization of somatosensory dendrites.
evidence: The claim is a summary statement supported by the preceding experimental observations.

claim: Sheath formation is first initiated on long-lived dendrite shafts in proximal portions of the dendrite arbor rather than the more dynamic distal portions of the dendrite arbor.
source: we found that sheath formation is first initiated on long-lived dendrite shafts in proximal portions of the dendrite arbor rather than the more dynamic distal portions of the dendrite arbor (Figure 6—figure supplement 2)
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data presented in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Terminal dendrites in general and newly formed terminal dendrites in particular were less extensively ensheathed than other portions of the dendrite arbor.
source: and that terminal dendrites in general and newly formed terminal dendrites in particular were less extensively ensheathed than other portions of the dendrite arbor (Figure 6P, Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data presented in Figure 6P and Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: New branch initiation occasionally occurred from ensheathed portions of dendrite arbors.
source: Consistent with prior observations (Han et al., 2012), we occasionally observed new branch initiation from ensheathed portions of dendrite arbors (Figure 6Q).
evidence: The claim is supported by time-lapse confocal microscopy data presented in Figure 6Q and a citation (Han et al., 2012).

claim: New branch initiation from ensheathed portions of dendrite arbors was rare and usually occurred at the ends of existing sheaths.
source: However, these events were rare and usually occurred at the ends of existing sheaths (Figure 6—figure supplement 3); the majority of new branch initiation occurred on unensheathed portions of dendrites.
evidence: The claim is supported by time-lapse confocal microscopy data presented in Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: The majority of new branch initiation occurred on unensheathed portions of dendrites.
source: However, these events were rare and usually occurred at the ends of existing sheaths (Figure 6—figure supplement 3); the majority of new branch initiation occurred on unensheathed portions of dendrites.
evidence: The claim is supported by time-lapse confocal microscopy data.

claim: A large proportion of new branches was formed in the vicinity of epithelial intercellular junctions.
source: Intriguingly, a large proportion of new branches was formed in the vicinity of epithelial intercellular junctions; whether this is simply a result of discontinuities in sheaths at intercellular junctions or reflects the function of non-autonomous branch-promoting activities associated with junctions remains to be determined.
evidence: The claim is supported by time-lapse confocal microscopy data. The use of 'whether' indicates speculation about the mechanism.

claim: Embryonic ablation of c4da neurons leads to exuberant dendrite growth in spared neurons beyond their normal boundaries to fill vacated territory.
source: Embryonic ablation of c4da neurons leads to exuberant dendrite growth in spared neurons beyond their normal boundaries to fill vacated territory (Grueber et al., 2003; Sugimura et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior published work (Grueber et al., 2003; Sugimura et al., 2003).

claim: The capacity of c4da neurons to expand their dendrite arbors beyond normal boundaries is progressively limited during development, concomitant with the increase in epidermal dendrite ensheathment.
source: This capacity of c4da neurons to expand their dendrite arbors beyond normal boundaries is progressively limited during development, concomitant with the increase in epidermal dendrite ensheathment (Parrish et al., 2009; Jiang et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior published work (Parrish et al., 2009; Jiang et al., 2014).

claim: Following ablation of a single c4da neuron at 72 h AEL, the spared neighboring neurons extend their dendrite arbors to cover 13% of the vacated territory, on average.
source: Following ablation of a single c4da neuron at 72 h AEL, the spared neighboring neurons extend their dendrite arbors to cover 13% of the vacated territory, on average (Figure 6R and U).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of confocal microscopy data presented in Figure 6R and 6U.

claim: Epidermis-specific PI4K(RNAi) or cora(RNAi) resulted in a significant potentiation of dendrite invasion following ablation of a neighboring c4da neuron.
source: Indeed, epidermis-specific PI4K(RNAi) or cora(RNAi) resulted in a significant potentiation of dendrite invasion (Figure 6S and U).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of confocal microscopy data presented in Figure 6S and 6U.

claim: Epidermal ensheathment contributes to the fidelity of receptive field coverage by coupling dendrite and epidermis expansion.
source: In addition to regulating the growth dynamics and elongation of individual terminal dendrites, these results suggest that epidermal ensheathment contributes to the fidelity of receptive field coverage by coupling dendrite and epidermis expansion.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that blocking ensheathment potentiates dendrite invasion following ablation.

claim: Harsh touch activates c4da nociceptive neurons to elicit stereotyped nocifensive rolling responses.
source: Harsh touch activates c4da nociceptive neurons to elicit stereotyped nocifensive rolling responses (Zhong et al., 2010)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior published work (Zhong et al., 2010).

claim: Stimulation with a 78 nM von Frey filament induced nociceptive rolling behavior in >60% of control larvae.
source: Stimulation with a 78 nM von Frey filament induced nociceptive rolling behavior in >60% of control larvae, whereas c4da-specific expression of the inward rectifying potassium channel Kir2.1 strongly attenuated this rolling response (Figure 7A).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral assay data presented in Figure 7A.

claim: C4da-specific expression of the inward rectifying potassium channel Kir2.1 strongly attenuated the rolling response to von Frey filament stimulation.
source: Stimulation with a 78 nM von Frey filament induced nociceptive rolling behavior in >60% of control larvae, whereas c4da-specific expression of the inward rectifying potassium channel Kir2.1 strongly attenuated this rolling response (Figure 7A).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral assay data presented in Figure 7A.

claim: Epidermal expression of PI4KIIIa(RNAi) significantly attenuated mechanonociceptive behavior.
source: Compared to controls, epidermal expression of either PI4KIIIa(RNAi) to block PIP2 accumulation or PIS(RNAi) to reduce phophoinositol biosynthesis, or feeding larvae the cell permeant polyphosphoinositide-binding peptide PBP10 to antagonize PIP2 signaling during the time window of sheath formation significantly attenuated mechanonociceptive behavior (Figure 7A, Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral assay data presented in Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Epidermal expression of PIS(RNAi) significantly attenuated mechanonociceptive behavior.
source: Compared to controls, epidermal expression of either PI4KIIIa(RNAi) to block PIP2 accumulation or PIS(RNAi) to reduce phophoinositol biosynthesis, or feeding larvae the cell permeant polyphosphoinositide-binding peptide PBP10 to antagonize PIP2 signaling during the time window of sheath formation significantly attenuated mechanonociceptive behavior (Figure 7A, Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral assay data presented in Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Feeding larvae the cell permeant polyphosphoinositide-binding peptide PBP10 to antagonize PIP2 signaling during the time window of sheath formation significantly attenuated mechanonociceptive behavior.
source: Compared to controls, epidermal expression of either PI4KIIIa(RNAi) to block PIP2 accumulation or PIS(RNAi) to reduce phophoinositol biosynthesis, or feeding larvae the cell permeant polyphosphoinositide-binding peptide PBP10 to antagonize PIP2 signaling during the time window of sheath formation significantly attenuated mechanonociceptive behavior (Figure 7A, Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral assay data presented in Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Epidermal expression of shiDN to block epidermal endocytosis attenuated mechanonociception.
source: Epidermal expression of shiDN to block epidermal endocytosis and cora(RNAi) to block sheath maturation similarly attenuated mechanonociception.
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral assay data.

claim: Epidermal expression of cora(RNAi) to block sheath maturation attenuated mechanonociception.
source: Epidermal expression of shiDN to block epidermal endocytosis and cora(RNAi) to block sheath maturation similarly attenuated mechanonociception.
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral assay data.

claim: Overexpressing α- and β-integrin in c4da neurons to tether dendrites to the ECM displayed reduced rolling rates in response to von Frey stimuli.
source: We additionally found that previously reported treatments that block ensheathment including overexpressing α- and β-integrin in c4da neurons to tether dendrites to the ECM (Han et al., 2012; Jiang et al., 2014) and mutation of the miRNA bantam (Jiang et al., 2014) displayed reduced rolling rates in response to von Frey stimuli.
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral assay data and citations (Han et al., 2012; Jiang et al., 2014).

claim: Mutation of the miRNA bantam displayed reduced rolling rates in response to von Frey stimuli.
source: We additionally found that previously reported treatments that block ensheathment including overexpressing α- and β-integrin in c4da neurons to tether dendrites to the ECM (Han et al., 2012; Jiang et al., 2014) and mutation of the miRNA bantam (Jiang et al., 2014) displayed reduced rolling rates in response to von Frey stimuli.
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral assay data and a citation (Jiang et al., 2014).

claim: Treatments that reduced epidermal sheath formation did not reduce larval stride length or crawling speed as would be expected for disruption of proprioceptor function, but instead led to increased larval crawling speed.
source: Treatments that reduced epidermal sheath formation did not reduce larval stride length or crawling speed as would be expected for disruption of proprioceptor function, but instead led to increased larval crawling speed (Figure 7B and data not shown).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral assay data presented in Figure 7B.

claim: The increased crawling speed in larvae with reduced epidermal sheath formation was largely the result of reduced turning frequency and a concomitant increase in forward-directed locomotion.
source: This increased crawling speed was largely the result of reduced turning frequency and a concomitant increase in forward-directed locomotion (Figure 7C), similar to defects in crawling trajectory induced by perturbing c4da function (Ainsley et al., 2003; Gorczyca et al., 2014)
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral assay data presented in Figure 7C and citations (Ainsley et al., 2003; Gorczyca et al., 2014).

claim: Epidermal ensheathment potentiates nociceptive mechanosensory responses.
source: Thus, epidermal ensheathment potentiates nociceptive mechanosensory responses and is apparently dispensable for proprioceptor function, consistent with our observation that nociceptive c4da but not proprioceptive c1da neurons exhibit extensive epidermal ensheathment.
evidence: The claim is a summary statement supported by the preceding experimental observations.

claim: Epidermal ensheathment is apparently dispensable for proprioceptor function.
source: Thus, epidermal ensheathment potentiates nociceptive mechanosensory responses and is apparently dispensable for proprioceptor function, consistent with our observation that nociceptive c4da but not proprioceptive c1da neurons exhibit extensive epidermal ensheathment.
evidence: The claim is a summary statement supported by the preceding experimental observations.
